questions.prompt: What is the interactor's job relative to entities?

options.text: It holds and enforces the domain rules itself
It orchestrates — coordinating steps and collaborators — while entities hold the domain rules
It formats data for the screen
It stores data in the database

questions.explanation: The interactor is a conductor: it orchestrates entities and gateways for one use case, while the entities enforce the actual domain rules.

questions.prompt: What may an interactor depend on? Select all that apply.

options.text: Interfaces it owns (gateways, the output boundary)

questions.explanation: An interactor depends only inward: on entities and interfaces it owns. Framework objects and ORM models are outer details it must not import.

questions.prompt: An interactor reports its result — success or failure — through an ______ boundary, so it never needs to know about the UI.
questions.explanation: The output boundary (output port) is an interface the interactor calls; a presenter implements it and decides how to display the result.

questions.prompt: Order the parts data flows through in a full interactor.
questions.explanation: A driver calls the input boundary with a request model; the interactor runs and reports via the output boundary with a response model.

questions.prompt: Match each concern to where it belongs.

pairs.left: Formatting the result for a screen

questions.explanation: General invariants live in entities; application-specific checks in the interactor; formatting in the presenter; SQL in the gateway.

questions.prompt: Why is a well-formed interactor easy to unit-test?

options.text: Because it imports the test framework directly
Because all its collaborators are interfaces, so tests supply in-memory fakes — no web server or database needed
Because it runs only in production

questions.explanation: Since every collaborator is an interface, a test injects in-memory fakes and a capturing output, exercising the rules with no framework or database.
